outcome: Heinrich, Kiyomi, Otachi, and Schweitzer proved (arXiv 2504.02353, submitted 3 April 2025, revised May 2026) that interval graphs with at least three vertices are reconstructible, settling this case of the reconstruction conjecture and giving a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm for that class; the general reconstruction conjecture and the new digraph reconstruction conjecture remain open. A separate, unrelated 2024 claim of a full proof (O'Shea & Wilkins) predates the frozen revision and remains undigested/unaccepted by the field.

disputes.summary: O'Shea and Wilkins, 'Vertex-substitution framework verifies the reconstruction conjecture for finite undirected graphs' (Information Sciences vol. 654, article 119858; made available online 2 November 2023, formally issued in the January 2024 print volume), claims a complete algebraic proof of the full reconstruction conjecture for finite undirected graphs. This claim predates the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) regardless of which of its two dates is used, so it cannot be the event this record's status rests on even if accepted. More importantly, as of September 2026 the claim has not been digested or endorsed by specialists: current surveys and the ProofAtlas tracking page for this conjecture continue to describe the general conjecture as open and record the O'Shea-Wilkins claim as an 'unverified resolution claim' rather than an accepted proof. No published refutation or counterexample to their argument was found either. This dispute is noted for completeness but does not change the record's status, since (a) it predates the window and (b) it remains undigested rather than accepted.

summary: Within the window (26 Jan 2024 – present) the clearest, verifiable change to this problem is Heinrich, Kiyomi, Otachi & Schweitzer's April 2025 arXiv preprint proving that interval graphs with at least three vertices are reconstructible (and reconstructible in polynomial time). This is a genuine case of the stated conjecture — interval graphs are a restriction of 'all graphs', so proving reconstructibility for them removes territory from the open general problem — and it has not (as far as I could establish) yet been digested by an independent expert account (no Tao-blog-level or journal-published discussion found), so it is classified 'partial' rather than 'resolved', resting on the preprint itself. No AI system is credited anywhere in this result; the authors' own account (per the arXiv abstract/HTML) describes purely human-derived combinatorial techniques. Separately, I found the most substantial AI-adjacent activity on this conjecture: Tsoukalas et al. (Google DeepMind, arXiv 2605.22763, 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search', submitted 21 May 2026), in which an AlphaEvolve-based agent 'helped formulate two bipartite variants of the graph reconstruction conjecture, along with a proposed full reconstruction algorithm' and 'produced a complete proof' for one of those variants, while only producing proof sketches/strategies for the other. Per the scope rule in §3.1, these are variants (bipartite incidence-deletion decks with different, self-formulated hypotheses such as biconnectivity and pairwise-distinct vertex types) rather than cases of the reconstruction conjecture as Wikipedia states it — they change the question rather than restrict it, and the agent itself devised the variants, which is a strong signal they are not simply narrower instances of the stated conjecture. I therefore do not let this AI work move the status, per the instruction that a related-problem result leaves status at 'open' (here 'partial', driven by the interval-graphs case) with the AI work noted as beside the question. I also verified O'Shea and Wilkins' 2024 Information Sciences paper claiming a full proof: it was made available online 2 November 2023 (DOI 10.1016/j.ins.2023.119858), before the frozen revision, so even if accepted it would be `open_stale`; but it is not accepted — ProofAtlas's tracking page and other 2026 sources still call the general conjecture open and describe the claim as unverified — so it does not change the status either way. The new digraph reconstruction conjecture: I found no result narrowing or resolving it in the window; it remains open per Wikipedia's own article and secondary sources (Ramachandran's 1979 conjecture, still open per the 'New digraph reconstruction conjecture' Wikipedia article as fetched). McKay's exhaustive verification up to 13 vertices predates the window and is unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind bipartite result should be coded as `ai_role: assisted` with `status: partial` if one reads 'a bipartite variant of the reconstruction conjecture' as a genuine case (e.g., if it can be shown that any counterexample to the stated conjecture restricted to bipartite graphs with the paper's extra hypotheses would also refute the general conjecture). I did not find the authors' precise theorem statement (the arXiv HTML excerpt did not include it), so I cannot rule out that their bipartite variant is literally a special case rather than a hypothesis-altered analogue. Given the paper's own language — 'AlphaEvolve experiments helped us formulate two bipartite variants' — and the added hypotheses (biconnected, pairwise-distinct vertex types) that are not merely 'graph is bipartite' but additional structural constraints changing the reconstruction problem (deck determines the graph 'up to bipartite graph isomorphism', a different equivalence than the original conjecture's graph isomorphism), I judge this to be a related problem rather than a case, but flag the ambiguity here since the full theorem text was not accessible to me.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full text (not just the HTML-extracted summary) of arXiv 2605.22763, once the companion paper 'currently in preparation' per the authors is posted, to see the exact statement of the bipartite reconstruction theorem and confirm whether it is a strict special case of graph reconstruction (same isomorphism notion, same deck definition, just restricted to a graph class) or a modified problem (different deck construction / different equivalence relation). Also, an expert digestion (journal acceptance or a survey/blog discussion) of the Heinrich–Kiyomi–Otachi–Schweitzer interval-graphs proof would upgrade its status from `partial` toward a more confidently 'expert-checked' partial result.
